props.title: Just One of the Girls

sections.content: Just One of the Guys (1985) - not "Just One of the Girls (1993)" (1993) - belongs to the gender-swap teen comedy wave of the 1980s, alongside films like Private School (1983) and Drive Me Crazy (1999). The film follows Joyce Hyser as Terry Griffith, a high school student who disguises herself as a male to prove her writing abilities aren't being taken seriously because of her gender. Like Tootsie (1982) and Mrs. Doubtfire (1993), it uses cross-dressing as both comedic device and social commentary, though aimed squarely at teen audiences.

sections.content: The 1980s and early 1990s saw numerous identity-swap comedies tackling gender politics through a mainstream lens. Big (1988) explored adult/child perspectives, while Vice Versa (1988) and Like Father Like Son (1987) played with parent-child body swaps. These films often used their high-concept premises to examine social roles and expectations, though rarely with the depth later films would attempt.

The gender-disguise trope evolved significantly by the late 1990s. She's the Man (2006) updated Twelfth Night with Amanda Bynes, while Yentl (1983) had already approached the concept with more gravity through Barbra Streisand's dramatic portrayal of a woman disguising herself to study Talmudic law. Boys Don't Cry (1999) marked a crucial shift toward examining genuine transgender experiences rather than using gender-swapping purely as comedy. SUBHEAD: Evolution of Gender Identity in Cinema

sections.content: The teen comedy landscape shifted dramatically from these earlier identity-swap films. While movies like Never Been Kissed (1999) still played with age and identity deception, later works like Mean Girls (2004) and Easy A (2010) tackled gender politics and identity more directly without requiring physical transformation plots. This evolution reflects changing social awareness and more nuanced approaches to gender representation in film.
